### Short summary

*What are the challenges and opportunities that can emerge from an agriculture without chemical pesticides in Sweden ?*

The use of chemical pesticides has been the main approach to limit crop yield losses to pests, pathogens and weeds in conventional agriculture.
However, the availability of such plant protection products is decreasing, as pests develop resistance, and as active substances posing threat to the environment and human health are being phased out.
Recent restrictions on chemical pesticides include for instance the neonicotinoid insecticides, in the European Union, and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), in Denmark. 
In 2026, the Swedish Plant Protection Council commissioned a report on the potential impacts of a withdrawal of trifluoroacetate-forming compounds in insecticides, expressing the need for actionable knowledge to support the agroecological transition of Swedish cropping systems.
Developing alternative plant protection strategies is crucial, but how a shift towards pest control strategies without chemical pesticides will affect crop yields is still largely uncertain.

Our project aims to address this knowledge gap, by 
(1) identifying which crops would be the most affected by a predicted reduction of chemical pesticides and 
(2) exploring the benefits and trade-offs of less chemically-dependent pest control alternatives.

To address our first objective, we will perform a vulnerability analysis of Swedish cropping systems to reduced access to chemical pesticides based on expert knowledge and pesticide trial data from the Nordic Field Trial System.
In a second phase, we will assess the potential of integrated pest control management strategies without chemical pesticides in most economically important crops and test their effects in two field studies.
The first field study will be conducted in 2027 and will investigate the efficiency of early-flowering cultivar mixture in limiting pest incidence in winter oilseed rape. 
In ten farmer fields distributed across Skåne, we will assess crop yield and damages caused by the cabbage stem flea beetle (*Psylliodes chrysocephala*), the pollen beetle (*Brassicogethes aeneus*), the cabbage stem weevil (*Ceutorhynchus pallidactylus*), the cabbage seed weevil (*Ceutorhynchus obstrictus*) and the brassica pod midge (*Dasineura brassicae*).
The second study will be conducted in 2028, and its focus will be determined by the outcome of the vulnerability assessment.
